title: The Fall of Tyre
overview: Ezekiel 28 pronounces a divine judgment against the prince and king of Tyre, exposing their pride and self-exaltation as they claim godlike status. The chapter vividly contrasts human arrogance with God’s sovereignty, revealing the downfall of a once-wise and wealthy ruler. It also contains a lamentation portraying the king of Tyre in exalted, almost angelic terms, symbolizing his original perfection and subsequent corruption. The chapter concludes with a prophecy against the city of Sidon and a promise of restoration and security for Israel. This chapter highlights the consequences of pride and rebellion against God, emphasizing His ultimate authority over nations and rulers.
structure:
**Verses 1-10: Judgment on the Prince of Tyre.** God commands Ezekiel to confront the prince of Tyre for his prideful claim to divinity and self-exaltation, warning of his impending downfall by foreign invaders.

**Verses 11-19: Lamentation for the King of Tyre.** A poetic and symbolic lament describes the king’s former perfection and beauty, likening him to a cherub in Eden, but also his fall due to iniquity and pride, resulting in his destruction.

**Verses 20-24: Prophecy Against Sidon.** God declares judgment against Sidon, promising to execute punishments that will demonstrate His holiness and power.

**Verses 25-26: Promise of Restoration for Israel.** The chapter closes with a hopeful promise that God will gather Israel from exile, sanctify them, and enable them to live securely in their land, free from surrounding enemies.

keyVerses.text: Son of man, say unto the prince of Tyrus, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Because thine heart is lifted up, and thou hast said, I am a God, I sit in the seat of God, in the midst of the seas; yet thou art a man, and not God, though thou set thine heart as the heart of God:
keyVerses.significance: This verse reveals the prince’s pride and blasphemous self-exaltation, setting the tone for the judgment. It underscores the fundamental biblical truth that no human is divine, emphasizing God’s exclusive sovereignty.

keyVerses.text: Thou art the anointed cherub that covereth; and I have set thee so: thou wast upon the holy mountain of God; thou hast walked up and down in the midst of the stones of fire.
keyVerses.significance: This verse uses rich imagery to depict the king of Tyre’s original exalted state, symbolizing purity and closeness to God. It highlights the tragic fall from perfection due to sin, illustrating the devastating effects of pride.

keyVerses.text: Thou hast defiled thy sanctuaries by the multitude of thine iniquities, by the iniquity of thy traffick; therefore will I bring forth a fire from the midst of thee, it shall devour thee, and I will bring thee to ashes upon the earth in the sight of all them that behold thee.
keyVerses.significance: This verse emphasizes the king’s corruption through sinful commerce and iniquity, resulting in divine judgment by fire. It vividly portrays God’s righteous punishment and public humiliation of the proud.

keyVerses.text: And there shall be no more a pricking brier unto the house of Israel, nor any grieving thorn of all that are round about them, that despised them; and they shall know that I am the Lord GOD.
keyVerses.significance: This verse promises the removal of enemies who have oppressed Israel, affirming God’s protective care and the eventual recognition of His sovereignty by all nations.

characters.name: Prince of Tyre
characters.description: A human ruler characterized by pride and arrogance, who claims to be divine. He represents human rebellion against God’s authority and faces judgment for his self-exaltation and reliance on wealth and wisdom.

characters.name: King of Tyre
characters.description: Portrayed symbolically as an anointed cherub, originally perfect and beautiful but corrupted by sin and pride. His fall illustrates the consequences of iniquity and the loss of divine favor.

characters.name: God (The LORD)
characters.description: The sovereign Judge who reveals the prince’s and king’s pride, pronounces judgment, and promises restoration for Israel. His holiness and authority are central to the chapter’s message.

characters.name: Sidon
characters.description: A neighboring city-state to Tyre, also subject to God’s judgment. Sidon’s punishment serves as a demonstration of God’s power and sanctification among the nations.

themes.description: The chapter vividly exposes the destructive nature of pride, especially when humans claim divine status. It connects to the biblical theme that God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.
God’s absolute authority over nations and rulers is affirmed throughout the chapter, reminding readers that no earthly power can rival His rule or escape His judgment.
The lamentation of the king of Tyre illustrates the biblical motif of the fall of the once-perfect being due to sin, paralleling themes of angelic rebellion and human failure.
Despite judgment on Tyre and Sidon, the chapter ends with a promise of Israel’s restoration and security, highlighting God’s faithfulness to His covenant people.

historicalContext: Ezekiel prophesied during the Babylonian exile (6th century BC), a time when the city-states of Phoenicia, including Tyre and Sidon, were influential maritime powers along the Mediterranean coast. Tyre was renowned for its wealth, commerce, and strategic location on an island, making it a formidable city-state. The political landscape was marked by shifting alliances and the dominance of empires such as Babylon. The pride and self-exaltation of Tyre’s rulers reflected their economic success and political power, but also their spiritual rebellion against Yahweh, the God of Israel. Understanding the geopolitical importance of Tyre and Sidon helps illuminate the severity of Ezekiel’s judgment and the hope offered to Israel amidst exile.

theologicalInterpretations.description: Reformed theologians see the prince and king of Tyre as emblematic of human pride and rebellion against God’s sovereignty. The cherub imagery is often interpreted as a reference to Satan’s original perfection and fall, emphasizing the spiritual dimension of pride and judgment.

Dispensationalists typically interpret the chapter as a dual prophecy: the prince and king of Tyre represent historical rulers, while the lamentation also symbolizes the fall of Satan. The future restoration of Israel is seen as literal, tied to end-times fulfillment.

Early Church Fathers often allegorized the king of Tyre as a figure of the devil, highlighting the spiritual pride that led to his downfall. They also emphasized God’s justice in punishing the proud and vindicating His people.

crossReferences.connection: This passage similarly describes the fall of a proud ruler, often linked to Satan, paralleling Ezekiel’s depiction of the king of Tyre’s pride and downfall.
Daniel’s wisdom is referenced in Ezekiel 28:3 to highlight the prince of Tyre’s arrogance, contrasting true godly wisdom with human pride.
The judgment on Tyre’s commerce and wealth in Ezekiel foreshadows the final judgment of Babylon the Great, a symbol of worldly pride and economic corruption.
This psalm describes the wickedness and pride of the ungodly, echoing the themes of iniquity and judgment found in Ezekiel 28.
Paul’s call to demolish proud arguments and take every thought captive connects with the chapter’s warning against prideful exaltation.

application: Recognize and confess pride in your heart, remembering that God alone is sovereign and worthy of worship.
Reject any temptation to elevate yourself above others or claim godlike status, cultivating humility instead.
Trust God’s justice when facing opposition or injustice, knowing He will vindicate His people in His timing.
Seek wisdom from God rather than relying solely on human understanding or wealth.
Pray for restoration and security for God’s people, trusting His promises of protection and provision.
Use the example of Tyre’s fall as a warning to guard against corruption and sinful commerce in your life.
conclusion: Ezekiel 28 powerfully confronts the dangers of pride and self-exaltation through the judgment of Tyre’s rulers, revealing the futility of claiming divine status apart from God. The chapter’s rich imagery and prophetic declarations underscore God’s absolute sovereignty and justice, while also offering hope through the promised restoration of Israel. For believers today, it serves as a solemn reminder to remain humble before God, to reject worldly arrogance, and to trust in His faithful care and ultimate authority over all nations and rulers.
timeline: c. 593-571 BC - Ezekiel’s prophetic ministry during the Babylonian exile

definitions.definition: The human ruler of the city-state of Tyre, addressed by Ezekiel for his pride and arrogance.
A high-ranking angelic being, symbolizing perfection and closeness to God, used here metaphorically for the king of Tyre.
Trade or commerce, especially referring to the extensive commercial activities of Tyre.
Holy places or temples; in this context, places defiled by the king’s iniquities.
A thorny plant causing pain or irritation, symbolizing enemies or troubles surrounding Israel.

outline.heading: Judgment on the Prince of Tyre

outline.heading: Lamentation for the King of Tyre
outline.description: A poetic lament describes the king’s former perfection and beauty, likening him to an anointed cherub, but also his fall due to sin and pride, culminating in his ruin.

outline.heading: Prophecy Against Sidon
outline.description: God pronounces judgment on Sidon, promising pestilence and sword, demonstrating His holiness and justice among the nations.

outline.heading: Promise of Restoration for Israel
